claim: Antimicrobial resistant determinants (ARDs) can be transmitted from livestock systems through meat products or environmental effluents.
source: Antimicrobial resistant determinants (ARDs) can be transmitted from livestock systems through meat products or environmental effluents.
evidence: This is a general statement about transmission pathways that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Over 300 unique ARDs were identified in the beef production system.
source: Over 300 unique ARDs were identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the metagenomic sequencing performed in the study.

claim: Resistome diversity decreased while cattle were in the feedlot.
source: Resistome diversity decreased while cattle were in the feedlot, indicating selective pressure.
evidence: This is supported by data from the study comparing arrival and exit samples.

claim: The decrease in resistome diversity during the feeding period indicates selective pressure.
source: Resistome diversity decreased while cattle were in the feedlot, indicating selective pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed decrease in resistome diversity.

claim: ARDs were not identified in beef products.
source: ARDs were not identified in beef products, suggesting that slaughter interventions may reduce the risk of transmission of ARDs to beef consumers.
evidence: This is based on data from post-slaughter samples analyzed in the study.

claim: Slaughter interventions may reduce the risk of transmission of ARDs to beef consumers.
source: ARDs were not identified in beef products, suggesting that slaughter interventions may reduce the risk of transmission of ARDs to beef consumers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of ARD detection in post-slaughter samples.

claim: Environmental pathways may represent a greater risk than the food supply for ARD transmission.
source: This report highlights the utility and limitations of metagenomics for assessing public health risks regarding antimicrobial resistance, and demonstrates that environmental pathways may represent a greater risk than the food supply.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding of ARDs in environmental samples but not in beef products.

claim: Beef is a widely consumed protein commodity.
source: Beef is a widely consumed protein commodity, and production and consumption is expected to increase in the United States and globally (Daniel et al., 2011; OECD/Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: Beef production and consumption is expected to increase in the United States and globally.
source: Beef is a widely consumed protein commodity, and production and consumption is expected to increase in the United States and globally (Daniel et al., 2011; OECD/Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to external sources.

claim: In North American beef production, several critically important antimicrobial drugs such as fluoroquinolones, macrolides and third-generation cephalosporins are used.
source: In North American beef production, several critically important antimicrobial drugs (AMDs) such as fluoroquinolones, macrolides and third-generation cephalosporins are used, while others are not, e.g., carbapenems (World Health Organization, 2011; Food and Drug Administration, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO and FDA sources.

claim: Carbapenems are not used in North American beef production.
source: In North American beef production, several critically important antimicrobial drugs (AMDs) such as fluoroquinolones, macrolides and third-generation cephalosporins are used, while others are not, e.g., carbapenems (World Health Organization, 2011; Food and Drug Administration, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO and FDA sources.

claim: Use of antimicrobial drugs is thought to increase the risk of AMR being transmitted to humans through environmental exposures.
source: Use of these AMDs is thought to increase the risk of AMR being transmitted to humans through environmental exposures (i.e., air, water and soil), occupational exposures (Levy et al., 1976; Moon et al., 2015), as well as through consumption of beef products (Antibiotic Resistance from the Farm to the Table [Internet], 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Use of antimicrobial drugs is thought to increase the risk of AMR being transmitted to humans through occupational exposures.
source: Use of these AMDs is thought to increase the risk of AMR being transmitted to humans through environmental exposures (i.e., air, water and soil), occupational exposures (Levy et al., 1976; Moon et al., 2015), as well as through consumption of beef products (Antibiotic Resistance from the Farm to the Table [Internet], 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Use of antimicrobial drugs is thought to increase the risk of AMR being transmitted to humans through consumption of beef products.
source: Use of these AMDs is thought to increase the risk of AMR being transmitted to humans through environmental exposures (i.e., air, water and soil), occupational exposures (Levy et al., 1976; Moon et al., 2015), as well as through consumption of beef products (Antibiotic Resistance from the Farm to the Table [Internet], 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Surveillance for foodborne AMR pathogens has been part of North American food safety systems for decades.
source: While surveillance for foodborne AMR pathogens has been part of North American food safety systems for decades (National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System – Enteric Bacteria (NARMS), 2011; Canadian Integrated Program for Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance (CIPARS), 2013), we have yet to fully understand and quantify the public health risk posed by transmission of non-pathogenic bacteria that carry antimicrobial resistance determinants (ARDs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to NARMS and CIPARS surveillance programs.

claim: The public health risk posed by transmission of non-pathogenic bacteria that carry antimicrobial resistance determinants is not yet fully understood.
source: While surveillance for foodborne AMR pathogens has been part of North American food safety systems for decades (National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System – Enteric Bacteria (NARMS), 2011; Canadian Integrated Program for Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance (CIPARS), 2013), we have yet to fully understand and quantify the public health risk posed by transmission of non-pathogenic bacteria that carry antimicrobial resistance determinants (ARDs).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: ARDs could pose a risk to human health if the bacteria carrying them become established within the microbiome of the human host, subsequently enabling horizontal gene transfer to pathogens.
source: These ARDs could pose a risk to human health if the bacteria carrying them become established within the microbiome of the human host, subsequently enabling horizontal gene transfer to pathogens (Forsberg et al., 2012; Rolain, 2013); or if these ARDs are present in opportunistic pathogens that become established within an immunocompromised individual.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on horizontal gene transfer.

claim: ARDs could pose a risk to human health if they are present in opportunistic pathogens that become established within an immunocompromised individual.
source: These ARDs could pose a risk to human health if the bacteria carrying them become established within the microbiome of the human host, subsequently enabling horizontal gene transfer to pathogens (Forsberg et al., 2012; Rolain, 2013); or if these ARDs are present in opportunistic pathogens that become established within an immunocompromised individual.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential health risks.

claim: Establishment of ARD-carrying bacteria within an individual's microbiome could occur through the ingestion of contaminated food products.
source: Establishment within an individual's microbiome could occur either through the ingestion of contaminated food products or through exposure to environmental effluents disseminated from beef feedlots (Antibiotic Resistance from the Farm to the Table [Internet], 2014), i.e., a facility where cattle are aggregated, reared in pens (i.e., outdoor enclosures) and fed a high-energy ration before being slaughtered.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a potential transmission pathway.

claim: Establishment of ARD-carrying bacteria within an individual's microbiome could occur through exposure to environmental effluents disseminated from beef feedlots.
source: Establishment within an individual's microbiome could occur either through the ingestion of contaminated food products or through exposure to environmental effluents disseminated from beef feedlots (Antibiotic Resistance from the Farm to the Table [Internet], 2014), i.e., a facility where cattle are aggregated, reared in pens (i.e., outdoor enclosures) and fed a high-energy ration before being slaughtered.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a potential transmission pathway.

claim: The rate at which ARDs from beef products or production facilities become established within humans is unknown.
source: The rate at which ARDs from beef products or production facilities become established within humans is unknown, largely due to an historical reliance on culture and isolation of pathogens and an inability to access the microbial community and its complete repertoire of ARDs (i.e., the resistome).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Use of antimicrobial drugs is much greater in feedlots than any other phase of beef production in North America.
source: In North America, use of AMDs is much greater in feedlots than any other phase of beef production (Gow et al., 2008; Rao et al., 2010), a fact that has raised concerns that these operations could represent the principal phase of beef production in which AMR is acquired or maintained.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Feedlots are intricately linked to environmental exposure pathways such as air, manure, soil, and water.
source: Furthermore, feedlots are intricately linked to environmental exposure pathways such as air, manure, soil, and water, enabling indirect human exposure to feedlot effluents (McEachran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Feedlots enable indirect human exposure to feedlot effluents.
source: Furthermore, feedlots are intricately linked to environmental exposure pathways such as air, manure, soil, and water, enabling indirect human exposure to feedlot effluents (McEachran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: North American abattoirs employ sequential antibacterial interventions to reduce pathogen contamination in beef products.
source: In North America, abattoirs (i.e., slaughterhouses) are a potential control point for the transmission of AMR , as they employ sequential antibacterial interventions to reduce pathogen contamination in beef products; testing of these interventions has demonstrated that they are effective in reducing not only pathogens, but also total bacterial contamination of beef products (Bacon et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Antibacterial interventions in abattoirs are effective in reducing pathogens and total bacterial contamination of beef products.
source: In North America, abattoirs (i.e., slaughterhouses) are a potential control point for the transmission of AMR , as they employ sequential antibacterial interventions to reduce pathogen contamination in beef products; testing of these interventions has demonstrated that they are effective in reducing not only pathogens, but also total bacterial contamination of beef products (Bacon et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A total of 1741 cattle were housed in 8 pens across 4 feedlots.
source: Pen capacities ranged from 150 to 281 cattle, and a total of 1741 cattle were housed in these 8 pens.
evidence: This is data from the study describing the sample population.

claim: The feeding period ranged from 117 to 227 days.
source: Antimicrobial exposures were recorded throughout the feeding period, i.e., the total time that animals were housed in the feedlot, which ranged from 117 to 227 days (see Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is data from the study describing the duration of the feeding period.

claim: All cattle received in-feed macrolides (tylosin).
source: Analysis of these records indicates that all cattle received in-feed macrolides (tylosin), but use of parenteral AMDs was relatively infrequent at the individual animal level (Table 1).
evidence: This is data from antimicrobial use records in the study.

claim: Use of parenteral antimicrobial drugs was relatively infrequent at the individual animal level.
source: Analysis of these records indicates that all cattle received in-feed macrolides (tylosin), but use of parenteral AMDs was relatively infrequent at the individual animal level (Table 1).
evidence: This is data from antimicrobial use records in the study.

claim: All pens contained at least one animal that was exposed to individual doses of parenteral tetracyclines and macrolides.
source: All pens contained at least one animal that was exposed to individual doses of parenteral tetracyclines and macrolides.
evidence: This is data from antimicrobial use records in the study.

claim: Total DNA was extracted from 88 samples and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq, resulting in 407.7 Gb of sequence data.
source: Total DNA was extracted from 88 samples and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq, resulting in 407.7 Gb of sequence data (average 46.3 M reads per sample, range 12.0–93.4 M, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is data describing the sequencing results from the study.

claim: The average number of reads per sample was 46.3 million.
source: Total DNA was extracted from 88 samples and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq, resulting in 407.7 Gb of sequence data (average 46.3 M reads per sample, range 12.0–93.4 M, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is data describing the sequencing results from the study.

claim: 319 unique ARDs were identified across all 87 samples.
source: We identified 319 unique ARDs across all 87 samples (Supplementary file 2), representing 1.2 M individual read alignments (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis in the study.

claim: The 319 ARDs identified represented 1.2 million individual read alignments.
source: We identified 319 unique ARDs across all 87 samples (Supplementary file 2), representing 1.2 M individual read alignments (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis in the study.

claim: Most ARDs were present in low numbers.
source: Most ARDs were present in low numbers (Figure 2A), and the proportion of trimmed, non-host reads aligning to ARDs in the database was correspondingly low across all samples (range 0.00% to 0.12%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The proportion of trimmed, non-host reads aligning to ARDs in the database ranged from 0.00% to 0.12% across all samples.
source: Most ARDs were present in low numbers (Figure 2A), and the proportion of trimmed, non-host reads aligning to ARDs in the database was correspondingly low across all samples (range 0.00% to 0.12%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis in the study.

claim: The median number of unique ARDs identified per sample was 33.
source: The median number of unique ARDs identified per sample was 33 (range: 0 to 136; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The range of unique ARDs identified per sample was 0 to 136.
source: The median number of unique ARDs identified per sample was 33 (range: 0 to 136; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A functional metagenomic study of dairy cattle feces reported a maximum of 26 unique ARDs per animal.
source: While this may be an underestimate due to sequencing coverage, recent studies using functional metagenomic screening of dairy cattle feces reported a maximum of 26 unique ARDs per animal (Wichmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Functional metagenomics offers increased sensitivity compared to shotgun metagenomics.
source: Functional metagenomics offers increased sensitivity compared to shotgun metagenomics (Forsberg et al., 2014), and therefore our observation of a relatively large number of unique ARDs per sample suggests that the pooling of samples undertaken in this study may have increased sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Pooling of samples in this study may have increased sensitivity for ARD detection.
source: Functional metagenomics offers increased sensitivity compared to shotgun metagenomics (Forsberg et al., 2014), and therefore our observation of a relatively large number of unique ARDs per sample suggests that the pooling of samples undertaken in this study may have increased sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with previous studies and the observed number of ARDs.

claim: A shotgun metagenomic study of 252 individual human fecal samples identified an average of 21 unique ARDs per sample.
source: For comparison, a shotgun metagenomic study of 252 individual human fecal samples identified an average of 21 unique ARDs per sample (Forslund et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The 319 ARDs identified represented 42 AMR mechanisms within 17 drug classes.
source: The 319 ARDs identified in this study represented 42 AMR mechanisms within 17 drug classes (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is data from the classification of ARDs in the study.

claim: Reads aligning to genes that encode resistance to tetracyclines and the macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin classes of antimicrobials were most abundant.
source: Reads aligning to genes that encode resistance to tetracyclines and the macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin classes of antimicrobials were most abundant, with the TetQ, TetW, TetO, and mefA gene families comprising the majority of alignments within these two classes (see Source Data for Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis in the study.

claim: The TetQ, TetW, TetO, and mefA gene families comprised the majority of alignments within tetracycline and macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin resistance classes.
source: Reads aligning to genes that encode resistance to tetracyclines and the macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin classes of antimicrobials were most abundant, with the TetQ, TetW, TetO, and mefA gene families comprising the majority of alignments within these two classes (see Source Data for Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis in the study.

claim: Pre-slaughter samples clustered by sample matrix based on ARD composition.
source: Pre-slaughter samples clustered by sample matrix (i.e., feces, soil, water and swabs, the latter of which comprised all truck samples) based on ARD composition (Figure 3A), suggesting that the resistomes in these sample types differed significantly.
evidence: This is supported by NMDS ordination results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The resistomes in different sample matrices (feces, soil, water, swabs) differed significantly.
source: Pre-slaughter samples clustered by sample matrix (i.e., feces, soil, water and swabs, the latter of which comprised all truck samples) based on ARD composition (Figure 3A), suggesting that the resistomes in these sample types differed significantly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering observed in NMDS ordination.

claim: Fecal samples exhibited a significant shift in resistome composition from arrival to exit or holding.
source: Therefore, to avoid confounding, we performed ordination separately on fecal, soil and water samples, all of which exhibited a significant shift from arrival to exit or holding (Figure 3B–D); the truck resistome could not be compared owing to complete confounding between sampling location and matrix type.
evidence: This is supported by NMDS ordination results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Soil samples exhibited a significant shift in resistome composition from arrival to exit.
source: Therefore, to avoid confounding, we performed ordination separately on fecal, soil and water samples, all of which exhibited a significant shift from arrival to exit or holding (Figure 3B–D); the truck resistome could not be compared owing to complete confounding between sampling location and matrix type.
evidence: This is supported by NMDS ordination results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Water samples exhibited a significant shift in resistome composition from arrival to exit or holding.
source: Therefore, to avoid confounding, we performed ordination separately on fecal, soil and water samples, all of which exhibited a significant shift from arrival to exit or holding (Figure 3B–D); the truck resistome could not be compared owing to complete confounding between sampling location and matrix type.
evidence: This is supported by NMDS ordination results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Culture-based studies of phenotypic resistance have reported mixed results when investigating potential associations between feedlot AMD use and AMR.
source: While this shift could result from AMD exposures, culture-based studies of phenotypic resistance have reported mixed results when investigating potential associations between feedlot AMD use and AMR (Rao et al., 2010; Morley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cattle undergo numerous changes during the feeding period, including maturation and a gradual shift from forage-based to high-energy rations.
source: In addition to AMD exposures, cattle undergo numerous changes during the feeding period, including maturation and a gradual shift from forage-based to high-energy rations, all of which have been shown to affect the fecal microbiome in swine, although little is known about these factors in beef cattle (Umu et al., 2015; Mach et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is general knowledge about cattle management practices.

claim: Maturation and dietary shifts have been shown to affect the fecal microbiome in swine.
source: In addition to AMD exposures, cattle undergo numerous changes during the feeding period, including maturation and a gradual shift from forage-based to high-energy rations, all of which have been shown to affect the fecal microbiome in swine, although little is known about these factors in beef cattle (Umu et al., 2015; Mach et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in swine.

claim: Little is known about the effects of maturation and dietary shifts on the fecal microbiome in beef cattle.
source: In addition to AMD exposures, cattle undergo numerous changes during the feeding period, including maturation and a gradual shift from forage-based to high-energy rations, all of which have been shown to affect the fecal microbiome in swine, although little is known about these factors in beef cattle (Umu et al., 2015; Mach et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Changes in bacterial community composition can drive changes in the resistome.
source: Therefore, changes in the resistome could also be driven by changes in bacterial community composition, a phenomenon recently reported for a set of functionally confirmed metagenomic soil samples (Forsberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There was high correlation between the resistome and the microbiome in arrival and exit samples.
source: This analysis confirmed a high correlation between the resistome (ARD level) and the microbiome (species level) in arrival and exit samples (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by procrustes analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: There was tighter correlation between the resistome and microbiome on arrival than on exit.
source: However, there was tighter correlation on arrival than on exit, leading to the hypothesis that additional factors such as AMD exposures may have influenced resistome changes independently of the microbiome.
evidence: This is supported by procrustes analysis results and leads to a hypothesis.

claim: Additional factors such as AMD exposures may have influenced resistome changes independently of the microbiome.
source: However, there was tighter correlation on arrival than on exit, leading to the hypothesis that additional factors such as AMD exposures may have influenced resistome changes independently of the microbiome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis generated from the observed differences in correlation.

claim: Resistome richness at the ARD level decreased significantly during the feeding period.
source: Resistome richness at the ARD level decreased significantly during the feeding period (Wilcoxon paired signed-rank p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The decrease in resistome richness occurred primarily through the loss of resistance to AMDs that were not used on cattle in this study population.
source: Interestingly, this decrease occurred primarily through the loss of resistance to AMDs that were not used on cattle in this study population or in the feeding systems in which they were raised (e.g., phenicols, aminocoumarins, elfamycins, rifampin, bacitracin and polymyxin B, Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Resistance to macrolides and tetracyclines remained prevalent in exit and holding pen samples.
source: In contrast, resistance to macrolides and tetracyclines remained prevalent in exit and holding pen samples, and these were the two classes of AMDs most commonly administered to cattle within study pens (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from the study.

claim: Macrolides and tetracyclines were the two classes of AMDs most commonly administered to cattle within study pens.
source: In contrast, resistance to macrolides and tetracyclines remained prevalent in exit and holding pen samples, and these were the two classes of AMDs most commonly administered to cattle within study pens (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by antimicrobial use data shown in Table 1.

claim: 5 of the 8 pens contained several cattle that received fluoroquinolones.
source: In addition, 5 of the 8 pens contained several cattle that received fluoroquinolones, and 3 of the 8 contained several cattle that received β-lactam AMDs.
evidence: This is data from antimicrobial use records in the study.

claim: 3 of the 8 pens contained several cattle that received β-lactam AMDs.
source: In addition, 5 of the 8 pens contained several cattle that received fluoroquinolones, and 3 of the 8 contained several cattle that received β-lactam AMDs.
evidence: This is data from antimicrobial use records in the study.

claim: The pattern of antimicrobial exposures during the feeding period may have created selective pressure that favored maintenance of ARDs conferring resistance to macrolides and tetracyclines.
source: One hypothesis for the finding of reduced ARD richness is that the pattern of antimicrobial exposures during the feeding period created pressure on microbes that favored maintenance of ARDs that conferred a fitness advantage (i.e., ARDs protecting against macrolides and tetracyclines).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data patterns.

claim: ARDs conferring resistance to antimicrobials that were not used in this study population may have exacted a fitness cost to bacteria carrying them.
source: Conversely, ARDs conferring resistance to antimicrobials that were not used in this study population (e.g., phenicols, aminocoumarins, elfamycins) or non-drug-specific ARDs (e.g., porin modification genes) did not confer a competitive advantage and may have exacted a fitness cost to bacteria carrying them (Vogwill and MacLean, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to previous research on fitness costs.

claim: Bacteria carrying ARDs that do not confer a competitive advantage may have gradually diminished in the population.
source: Thus, such bacteria may have gradually diminished in the population, leading to disappearance of these ARDs within the pan-microbial population and thus an observed decrease in ARD richness.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed decrease in ARD richness.

claim: Aminoglycoside resistance remained prevalent throughout the feeding period despite the absence of these drugs in this study population.
source: Interestingly, the aminoglycoside class was an exception to this pattern, as aminoglycoside resistance remained prevalent throughout the feeding period despite the absence of these drugs in this study population and in beef production in general.
evidence: This is an observation from the data that contradicts the general pattern.

claim: Aminoglycosides are not used in beef production in general.
source: Interestingly, the aminoglycoside class was an exception to this pattern, as aminoglycoside resistance remained prevalent throughout the feeding period despite the absence of these drugs in this study population and in beef production in general.
evidence: This is general knowledge about antimicrobial use in beef production.

claim: The relationship between AMD use and AMR is not straightforward.
source: While this study was not designed to definitely test for AMD-ARD associations, these findings suggest that the relationship between AMD use and AMR is not straightforward.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns in the data.

claim: An arrival soil sample contained the functionally-confirmed carbapenemase (bla)OXA-235.
source: An arrival soil sample contained the functionally-confirmed carbapenemase (bla)OXA-235 (Higgins et al., 2013) as well as vgaD and vatG ARDs, which together confer resistance to quinupristin-dalfopristin (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis, with citation supporting functional confirmation.

claim: An arrival soil sample contained vgaD and vatG ARDs, which together confer resistance to quinupristin-dalfopristin.
source: An arrival soil sample contained the functionally-confirmed carbapenemase (bla)OXA-235 (Higgins et al., 2013) as well as vgaD and vatG ARDs, which together confer resistance to quinupristin-dalfopristin (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis, with citation supporting the resistance mechanism.

claim: Another arrival soil sample and a water sample from a holding pen contained (bla)OXA-347.
source: Another arrival soil sample and a water sample from a holding pen contained (bla)OXA-347, which has only been shown to confer resistance to ampicillin but is classified as a carbapenemase based on 53% amino acid identity (Cheng et al., 2012); therefore, it is unknown whether this is a true carbapenemase ARD.
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis.

claim: (bla)OXA-347 has only been shown to confer resistance to ampicillin but is classified as a carbapenemase based on 53% amino acid identity.
source: Another arrival soil sample and a water sample from a holding pen contained (bla)OXA-347, which has only been shown to confer resistance to ampicillin but is classified as a carbapenemase based on 53% amino acid identity (Cheng et al., 2012); therefore, it is unknown whether this is a true carbapenemase ARD.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is unknown whether (bla)OXA-347 is a true carbapenemase ARD.
source: Another arrival soil sample and a water sample from a holding pen contained (bla)OXA-347, which has only been shown to confer resistance to ampicillin but is classified as a carbapenemase based on 53% amino acid identity (Cheng et al., 2012); therefore, it is unknown whether this is a true carbapenemase ARD.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty regarding the functional classification of this ARD.

claim: 3 of 7 water samples collected from holding pens contained reads aligning to the strict carbapenemase class bla(cphA).
source: Of the 7 sequenced water samples collected from holding pens, 3 contained reads aligning to the strict carbapenemase class bla(cphA).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis.

claim: The 4 truck samples collected in Texas all contained a CfrA 23S rRNA methyltransferase.
source: Additionally, the 4 truck samples collected in Texas all contained a CfrA 23S rRNA methyltransferase, which confers resistance to phenicols, lincosamides, oxazolidinones (linezolid), pleuromutilins, and streptogramin A (PhLOPSA).
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis.

claim: CfrA 23S rRNA methyltransferase confers resistance to phenicols, lincosamides, oxazolidinones (linezolid), pleuromutilins, and streptogramin A.
source: Additionally, the 4 truck samples collected in Texas all contained a CfrA 23S rRNA methyltransferase, which confers resistance to phenicols, lincosamides, oxazolidinones (linezolid), pleuromutilins, and streptogramin A (PhLOPSA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the resistance mechanism of CfrA.

claim: Study cattle were not exposed to aminoglycosides, carbapenems, streptogramins, phenicols, lincosamides, linezolid, or pleuromutilins while in the feedlot.
source: Despite the presence of these ARDs, study cattle were not exposed to aminoglycosides, carbapenems, streptogramins, phenicols, lincosamides, linezolid, or pleuromutilins while in the feedlot (Table 1).
evidence: This is data from antimicrobial use records in the study.

claim: Carbapenems, pleuromutilins and linezolid are not approved for use in cattle production.
source: In addition, carbapenems, pleuromutilins and linezolid are not approved for use in cattle production, and therefore antimicrobial use practices cannot directly explain the presence of these important ARDs.
evidence: This is knowledge about regulatory approval of antimicrobials in cattle production.

claim: Antimicrobial use practices cannot directly explain the presence of ARDs to carbapenems, pleuromutilins and linezolid.
source: In addition, carbapenems, pleuromutilins and linezolid are not approved for use in cattle production, and therefore antimicrobial use practices cannot directly explain the presence of these important ARDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of use of these drugs in cattle production.

claim: bla(TEM)-116, an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) ARD, was identified in 1 water holding pen sample.
source: We also identified bla(TEM)-116, an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) ARD, in 1 water holding pen sample.
evidence: This is data from the metagenomic analysis.

claim: Third-generation cephalosporins are used in beef cattle production.
source: Third-generation cephalosporins (a class of β-lactams) are used in beef cattle production, although other drugs are often used more commonly as reflected in this study (Table 1).
evidence: This is general knowledge about antimicrobial use in beef cattle production.

claim: Other drugs are often used more commonly than third-generation cephalosporins in beef cattle production.
source: Third-generation cephalosporins (a class of β-lactams) are used in beef cattle production, although other drugs are often used more commonly as reflected in this study (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and general knowledge.

claim: ARDs from the bla(SHV), bla(CTX-M) or bla(CMY) classes of ESBLs were not identified.
